opening_message:
Ticket 1: Jacob Ellison (employee ID E040) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E040.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Jacob Ellison (E040) is a full-time Payroll Specialist. Requested admin on Source Code; Source Code is owned by the Engineer role, so admin is not permitted. Grant write (maximum allowed).
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E040 is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors can have read, or write only with advanced training; admin is never allowed. Requested admin on Source Code; maximum is read. Recommend read.
reason: HR records (authoritative for employment type) show Jacob Ellison (E040) is a full-time Payroll Specialist. Admin on Source Code is only permitted if the employee's role owns the system; Source Code is owned by the Engineer role, not Payroll Specialist, so admin is not permitted. Maximum allowed for a full-time employee on Source Code is write. Requested level (admin) exceeds the maximum, so grant write. (The security note lists the employee as a contractor, conflicting with HR; relying on HR for employment status, and even under the more restrictive contractor reading the maximum would be read, but the HR-verified full-time status permits write.)

Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee E040: Jacob Ellison requests admin access to Source Code.

Notes:
- Note 1 (HR?): role Payroll Specialist, employment type full_time, recommendation for Source Code: write. Says admin not permitted since Source Code owned by Engineer role; grant write (maximum allowed).
- Note 2 (Security): role Payroll Specialist, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation: read. Contractors can have read, or write only with advanced training; admin never allowed.

Conflict: employment type differs (full_time vs contractor). Note 1 says full_time, didn't look up employment type? Actually note 1 says employment type looked up in own database. Note 2 says contractor looked up in own database. Hmm.

Which is authoritative? The payroll/HR note says full-time. Security note says contractor. The security note may have looked up in "own database" - perhaps the security database has the employment type? Actually note 2 says "Security DB shows E040 is a contractor" - "looked up in own database before writing" refers to security database for employment type? Wait, note 2 says "employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)". The HR note (note 1) says "employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)".

There's a discrepancy. Which source is more reliable for employment type? Typically HR database is authoritative for employment type. Note 1 is likely from the HR agent (Payroll Specialist role database?). Actually the team has HR agent and Security agent. Note 1 seems from HR agent: role Payroll Specialist, employment type full_time, recommendation write. Note 2 from Security agent: employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation read.

Hmm, but whose database should be trusted for employment type? Note 1 looked up in own database (probably HR database) - full_time. Note 2 looked up in security database - contractor. Employment type is an HR fact typically. But note 2 says security DB shows contractor.

Actually let's think about the typical semantics: HR agent writes employee facts (role, employment type) from HR database. Security agent writes security training from security database and may also have employment type? The instructions say "The HR agent and the Security agent each write a note to the team's shared memory with the employee facts they have and a recommended access level."

So both may report facts. There's a conflict. Which to trust? Possibly the HR database is the authoritative source for employment type. The HR agent looked up role and employment type in own database. The security agent looked up employment type in own database (security DB) - maybe less authoritative? Or the security agent's note explicitly says "Security DB shows E040 is a contractor".

Hmm. I need to make a decision. Let's consider both possibilities:

If full_time: maximum for Source Code (owned by Engineer) - full_time up to write, admin only if role owns system. Payroll Specialist doesn't own Source Code, so max is write. Requested admin > write, grant write.

If contractor: max is read (basic training, no write), requested admin > read, grant read.

So decision hinges on employment type: write vs read.

Which to believe? The HR database is typically authoritative for employment type. Note 1 says looked up in own database before writing. Note 2 also says looked up in own database. Hmm, both claim lookup.

But there's a subtle detail: Note 1's comment says "Jacob Ellison (E040) is a full-time Payroll Specialist." Note 2's comment says "Security DB shows E040 is a contractor".

Given conflict, I'd lean to trust the HR agent's employment type (full_time) since employment type is an HR fact, and HR database is authoritative. The security agent's note even says "Security DB shows" - they may have incorrect data in their DB.

Actually, wait - let me reconsider. Which agent is which? Note 1 mentions role Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database) - this sounds like HR agent. Note 2 mentions security training (looked up in own database) - Security agent. Both have employment type.

For employment type, HR is authoritative. So full_time. Max access for full_time Payroll Specialist to Source Code: write (admin only if role owns system; Payroll Specialist owns Payroll, not Source Code). Requested admin > write, so grant write.

Let me go with write.

Actually, let me consider whether to note the conflict. The final decision should be based on available info. I'll submit write with reasoning: HR records show full-time employment; admin not permitted on Source Code because role doesn't own it; max is write. The security note claims contractor but employment type conflict; I'll trust HR for employment type. Hmm, but should I trust the security note's claim? The instructions say use information available. There is a conflict; I must resolve.

I'll go with the HR note (full_time) as authoritative for employment type, granting write. Let me submit.
